source.title: LLM Unlearning with LLM Beliefs
source.authors: Ke-Mou Li; Qi-Zhou Wang; Yue Wang; Feng-Peng Li; Jun Liu; Bo Han; Jian-Tao Zhou

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present. Some extracted figure axes are garbled, so their plotted values cannot be read reliably.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own evidence that GA/NPO can leave semantically related knowledge in generated responses, and argues that this makes their apparent forgetting partial or spurious. It also evaluates unlearning and retention on WMDP and other benchmarks.
record.gate_note: The paper does not test fine-tuning recovery attacks, activation-direction ablation, quantization, or prompt-rephrasing/jailbreak attacks. Its discussion of paraphrases concerns outputs generated after ordinary evaluation prompts, not recovery induced by rephrasing the prompts. Results cited from other work are not recorded as rows. Figure-based probability and similarity trends are included only where the paper describes them in text.
record.test_reason: The study argues, with its own LaaJ similarity results and greedy outputs, that NPO's metric-reported forgetting on TOFU is spurious: paraphrased outputs still carry the target facts. It also reports forgetting and retention for several methods on WMDP and MUSE, which bears on version A's near-chance-plus-retention part. It runs no recovery attacks (fine-tuning, ablation, quantization, prompting). Its paraphrase finding comes from ordinary forget prompts, not rephrased prompts.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, with one correction. GA fails by collapsing into degenerate output; NPO-style methods yield spurious forgetting, suppressing exact targets while paraphrases keep the content (the squeezing effect). The authors conclude that bootstrapping on the model's own high-confidence tokens (BS-T) or sequences (BS-S) mitigates this. They report better forgetting-retention trade-offs on TOFU, MUSE and WMDP.
record.recipe_differences: The paper evaluates established unlearning baselines and introduces BS-T/BS-S, which add model-belief signals to the unlearning objective. It does not reproduce the recovery attacks described in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by unlearning method, benchmark, model, and forget percentage. The authors also report BS-T sensitivity to its bootstrapping coefficient and BS-S sensitivity to its coefficient and sample count.

fits_no_version.finding: During GA and NPO training, lowering the target's probability raises the probability of the model's high-likelihood paraphrases. Under NPO this persists; under GA it collapses as the model degrades.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient-ascent-style unlearning redistributes probability mass to semantically similar high-likelihood rephrasings (the squeezing effect), leaving the knowledge expressible.

record.problems: No recovery attacks or activation ablation are tested, so the study cannot establish resistance to the attacks in the claim. Some mechanistic trends are only plotted and their numeric values are not extractable here. Several evaluations are benchmark-specific; the paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the tabulated results.
record.rows_left_out: The 60-row limit was reached. Omitted results include the remaining model-by-forget-fraction and method rows from TOFU Table 1, MUSE-News Table 4, additional WMDP baseline comparisons, and supplementary qualitative examples and ablations. These were left out after retaining WMDP method/metric rows, MUSE-Books method/metric rows, the TOFU aggregate values explicitly highlighted in the text, and the direct mechanistic results.

untested.parts: Whether simple attacks fail to recover the knowledge; no attack is run.
No activation-direction ablation. No analysis showing blocked access versus deletion; the squeezing analysis concerns redistribution to paraphrases in ordinary outputs.
No rephrased, jailbreak, multilingual or in-context prompts.
BS-T/BS-S are not tested against any recovery attack.

missing.what: LaaJ Naturalness and Similarity scores comparing GradDiff, NPO, SimNPO, RMU, BS-T and BS-S after unlearning (Gemini 2.5 Flash judge, Llama 3.1 8B). This bears on how much semantic knowledge each method leaves; the values are only plotted.
Qualitative outputs from GradDiff, SimNPO and WGA that also restate forgotten facts (e.g. 'English', India settings). These show that spurious forgetting extends beyond NPO; the rows cover NPO only.

record.verdict_notes: The record linked the squeezing and paraphrase rows to C. They are relinked to A, because they show the knowledge is not removed in ordinary outputs, not hidden-then-recovered by internal edits. Agg. rows are composites and marked cannot_determine. Retrain rows are oracle references. No uncertainty is reported, and hyperparameters are tuned per method by grid search.

versions.untested_parts: The study evaluates forgetting and retention, including WMDP accuracy and MMLU, but does not test whether simple attacks fail to recover the knowledge.
No recovery fine-tuning using unrelated, loosely related, or subset examples.
The study analyzes probability redistribution and paraphrased outputs for GA/NPO; it does not ablate an activation direction.
No prompt-rephrasing, jailbreak, multilingual, or in-context-information recovery attack.
The proposed BS-T and BS-S methods are evaluated for unlearning, but not against the recovery attacks named in the claim.
